xhosa-kingdom.t: The united Xhosa paramountcy of the Tshawe royal house, which expanded westward to meet the Cape Colony's frontier before splitting in two.
xhosa-kingdom.o: The [[e:xhosa-people|Xhosa]] were the south-westernmost [[e:nguni|Nguni-speaking]] people, and their royal Tshawe lineage traditionally asserted supremacy over other clans in the region between the [[e:mbashe-river|Mbashe]] and Kei rivers. By the 17th century the Xhosa paramount was recognised by a growing confederation of chiefdoms, many incorporating [[e:khoekhoe|Khoikhoi]] groups.
xhosa-kingdom.r: The paramount ruled through royal kin who governed their own chiefdoms with considerable independence, advised by councils of counsellors. Wealth was measured in [[e:cattle|cattle]], and expansion came through younger sons founding new chiefdoms in fresh pastures. Under [[e:tshiwo|Tshiwo]] and [[e:phalo|Phalo]] the [[e:xhosa-people|Xhosa]] moved west towards the [[e:great-fish-river|Fish River]], absorbing [[e:khoekhoe|Khoikhoi]] and gaining clicks in their language.
xhosa-kingdom.e: A dispute between [[e:phalo|Phalo's]] sons [[s:gcaleka-xhosa-kingdom|Gcaleka]] and [[s:rharhabe-xhosa-kingdom|Rharhabe]] split the paramountcy, and on Phalo's death around 1775 it divided into the Gcaleka [[e:xhosa-people|Xhosa]] Kingdom east of the Kei and the Rharhabe Xhosa Kingdom to the west, just as frontier wars with the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]] began.

xianbei.t: The nomadic confederation that replaced the Xiongnu on the Mongolian steppe, whose clans later founded the Northern Wei and other dynasties of northern China.
xianbei.o: The Xianbei were descendants of the [[s:donghu|Donghu]] who fled to the Xianbei mountains in the north-east after the [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]] destroyed them around 206 BCE. For two centuries they lived under Xiongnu domination in eastern [[e:inner-mongolia|Inner Mongolia]] and [[e:manchuria|Manchuria]]. When Han armies broke the [[s:northern-xiongnu|Northern Xiongnu]] in 87 to 91 CE, the Xianbei moved west and absorbed tens of thousands of Xiongnu households.
xianbei.r: Around 156 CE the chieftain Tanshihuai united the tribes into a confederation stretching from [[e:manchuria|Manchuria]] to the borders of the [[s:wusun|Wusun]], divided into eastern, central and western sections, and raided the [[s:han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] frontier almost yearly. They lived as mounted herders and probably spoke an early Mongolic language. Power depended on the prestige of individual leaders rather than a fixed dynasty.
xianbei.e: Tanshihuai's confederation broke up after his death around 181. The chieftain [[e:kebineng|Kebineng]] rebuilt a large federation until [[s:cao-wei|Cao Wei]] agents assassinated him in 235. Xianbei clans such as the [[e:murong-xianbei|Murong]], [[e:tuoba|Tuoba]], [[s:duan-xianbei|Duan Xianbei]] and [[s:yuwen-xianbei|Yuwen Xianbei]] went on to found states including the [[s:northern-wei|Northern Wei]].

xochimilco.t: A Nahua altepetl on the southern lakes of the Valley of Mexico, famed for its chinampa gardens, conquered by the Mexica around 1430.
xochimilco.o: The Xochimilca were one of the [[e:nahuas|Nahua]] groups said to have migrated from [[e:aztlan|Aztlan]] and settled in the southern [[e:valley-of-mexico|Valley of Mexico]] in the 12th or 13th century. They established Xochimilco on the shores of [[e:lake-xochimilco|Lake Xochimilco]] around 1200.
xochimilco.r: Xochimilco was ruled by its own tlatoque and controlled a domain stretching into the hills of [[e:morelos|Morelos]]. Its people were masters of chinampa farming, building raised fields of mud and vegetation in the shallow lake, which produced [[e:maize|maize]], vegetables and flowers in abundance. Their stonework and gardening skill were valued by neighbouring cities.
xochimilco.e: After the fall of the [[s:tepanec-empire|Tepanec Empire]], [[e:itzcoatl|Itzcoatl's]] [[e:mexica|Mexica]] forces conquered Xochimilco around 1430 and made it a tributary of the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]], using its labour to build the causeway to [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]]. Its [[e:chinampa|chinampas]] survive and are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

xia-dynasty.t: China's traditional first dynasty, founded by the flood-taming Yu the Great; whether it was a real state remains one of the great open questions of Chinese archaeology.
xia-dynasty.o: Later histories, above all [[e:sima-qian|Sima Qian's]] [[e:records-of-the-grand-historian|Records of the Grand Historian]], describe the Xia as the dynasty founded when [[e:yu-the-great|Yu the Great]], rewarded for controlling the floods of the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]], passed power to his son Qi, making rule hereditary. The register follows the [[e:xia-shang-zhou-chronology-project|Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project]]'s dates. No writing survives from the period itself.
xia-dynasty.r: Everything known comes from texts written a thousand years later or from archaeology. Many scholars link the Xia with the [[e:erlitou-culture|Erlitou culture]] of the [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] basin in [[e:henan|Henan]], which built palace compounds on rammed-earth platforms, cast the earliest Chinese bronze ritual vessels and made jade blades. Whether Erlitou was the Xia, and what its people called themselves, cannot be proved without inscriptions.
xia-dynasty.e: Tradition holds that the last king, [[e:jie-of-xia|Jie]], was a tyrant overthrown by [[s:later-tang|Tang]], founder of the [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang dynasty]], at the [[e:battle-of-mingtiao|Battle of Mingtiao]]. The Xia became the model of the first legitimate dynasty, and later Chinese political thought used its fall as the classic example of [[e:tian|Heaven]] withdrawing its favour from a corrupt ruler.

xueyantuo.t: A Tiele tribe that briefly ruled the Mongolian steppe after the fall of the Eastern Turks, before Tang China destroyed it in 646.
xueyantuo.o: The Xueyantuo were one of the [[e:tiele|Tiele]] tribes of the steppe, subject to the Turkic [[e:khagan|khagans]]. In 628 they rebelled against the [[s:eastern-turkic-khaganate|Eastern Turkic Khaganate]] under their leader [[e:zhenzhu-khagan|Yinan]], who was recognised by [[e:emperor-taizong-of-tang|Tang Taizong]] as Zhenzhu Khagan. After the Turks fell in 630 they became the dominant power in [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]].
xueyantuo.r: [[e:zhenzhu-khagan|Zhenzhu Khagan]] ruled a confederation of [[e:tiele|Tiele]] tribes including the [[e:uyghurs|Uyghurs]], and could reportedly field 200,000 horsemen. He balanced between alliance and rivalry with the [[s:later-tang|Tang]], negotiating a marriage alliance that [[e:emperor-taizong-of-tang|Taizong]] ultimately cancelled, and clashed with Turks resettled by the Tang south of the [[e:gobi-desert|Gobi]].
xueyantuo.e: After [[e:zhenzhu-khagan|Zhenzhu Khagan's]] death in 645, his son [[e:duomi-khagan|Duomi Khagan]] attacked [[s:later-tang|Tang]] territory. In 646 a Tang army, aided by the [[e:uyghurs|Uyghurs]] and other [[e:tiele|Tiele]] tribes, destroyed the Xueyantuo. Their lands came under Tang [[e:protectorate|protectorates]], and the Uyghurs later rose to dominate the same region.

xin-dynasty.t: The single-reign dynasty of Wang Mang, the Han regent who seized the throne in 9 CE to remake China on ancient models and died as his capital burned.
xin-dynasty.o: [[e:wang-mang|Wang Mang]] rose through his aunt, the Han empress dowager [[e:wang-zhengjun|Wang Zhengjun]], and became regent for child emperors of the [[s:han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]]. Presenting himself as a Confucian sage and citing omens, he accepted the abdication of the last infant ruler and proclaimed the Xin, 'New', dynasty in 9 CE, ruling from [[e:changan|Chang'an]].
xin-dynasty.r: [[e:wang-mang|Wang Mang]] tried to restore the institutions described in the [[e:rites-of-zhou|Rites of Zhou]]. He declared all land the king's land, banned the sale of land and slaves, created state monopolies and price controls, and repeatedly changed the coinage, reviving knife-shaped coins. The reforms disrupted the economy, and shifts in the course of the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]] around 11 CE brought flooding and famine.
xin-dynasty.e: Peasant risings such as the [[e:red-eyebrows|Red Eyebrows]] and the [[e:lulin|Lülin]] spread. In 23 rebels broke into [[e:changan|Chang'an]] and killed [[e:wang-mang|Wang Mang]]. [[e:emperor-guangwu-of-han|Liu Xiu]], a Han kinsman, restored the dynasty in 25 as Emperor Guangwu, beginning the [[e:han-dynasty|Eastern Han]].
xin-dynasty.re: Confucian state ritual and ancestral religion

xochicalco.t: A fortified hilltop city in Morelos that flourished after Teotihuacan's fall, famed for its Temple of the Feathered Serpent.
xochicalco.o: Xochicalco was built around 650 on a group of hills in western [[e:morelos|Morelos]], as power in central [[s:mexico|Mexico]] fragmented after the decline of [[s:teotihuacan|Teotihuacan]]. Its position allowed control of trade routes between the [[e:valley-of-mexico|Valley of Mexico]], [[e:guerrero|Guerrero]] and the [[e:gulf-coast-of-mexico|Gulf Coast]].
xochicalco.r: The city was terraced, walled and moated, with three ballcourts, palaces and an observatory cave where a shaft allowed sunlight to mark the zenith passages of the sun. The [[e:temple-of-the-feathered-serpent-xochicalco|Temple of the Feathered Serpent]] carries reliefs of plumed serpents and seated figures in Maya-like style, with glyphs that some scholars read as a calendar correction meeting. Artisans worked obsidian and other goods for trade.
xochicalco.e: Xochicalco was burnt and abandoned around 900. Its ideas, such as feathered-serpent imagery, passed to the later [[s:toltec-state|Toltec state]]. It became a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1999.

xia-dou-jiande.t: The rebel kingdom of Dou Jiande on the Hebei plain, remembered as the most humane of the Sui-era insurgent regimes, destroyed at the Battle of Hulao in 621.
xia-dou-jiande.o: [[e:dou-jiande|Dou Jiande]], a village headman from Zhangnan in [[e:hebei|Hebei]], joined the peasant risings against [[e:emperor-yang-of-sui|Emperor Yang's]] levies for the [[s:goguryeo|Goguryeo]] wars in 611. He took over the band of [[e:gao-shida|Gao Shida]], proclaimed himself Prince of Changle in 617 and Prince of Xia in 618, ruling much of Hebei from Lezhou.
xia-dou-jiande.r: [[e:dou-jiande|Dou Jiande]] won a reputation for frugality, for sparing captured [[e:sui-dynasty|Sui]] officials and employing them in his government, and for sharing spoils with his soldiers. In 619 he defeated and executed [[e:yuwen-huaji|Yuwen Huaji]], the murderer of [[e:emperor-yang-of-sui|Emperor Yang]], which raised his standing among loyalists of the [[s:sui-dynasty|Sui Dynasty]].
xia-dou-jiande.e: In 621 he marched to relieve [[e:wang-shichong|Wang Shichong]], besieged at [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] by the [[s:later-tang|Tang]]. [[e:emperor-taizong-of-tang|Li Shimin]] blocked him at the [[e:battle-of-hulao|Hulao]] pass and captured him; he was executed at [[e:changan|Chang'an]]. His former officers under [[e:liu-heita|Liu Heita]] rose again and held out until 623.
